findings.text: Transgression is explicitly defined as law-relative, not free-standing. Rom 4:15 states this almost as a formal rule: where there is no law there is no transgression (G3847): the concept requires a prior boundary to cross.

Both root words for transgress in this family are spatial-boundary words: G3845 (parabainō, step past) and H5674D (avar, pass over, through or by). H5674D's meaning block runs 25 senses, nearly all literal motion (crossing a river, passing a border, a passer-by), with the moral sense of transgressing a covenant or command appearing as one derived branch among many (Judg 2:20, Dan 9:11, Hos 6:7). The metaphor is the same across both languages: sin as a line stepped over.

One violation voids the whole standard: the same argument recurs from the guilt subgroup. G3848's Jas 2:11 (if you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law) is the identical argument already found under G1777 in the guilt subgroup (Jas 2:10, become guilty of all of it): the same author applying the same whole-law-is-one-unit logic to two different M10 gloss-families independently.

G3900 (paraptōma, trespass) is defined more by its remedy than by the act: it is Paul's central Adam and Christ contrast term (Rom 5:15-20) and is otherwise almost entirely a forgiveness-context word: forgive their trespasses (Matt 6:14-15, Eph 1:7, Col 2:13), not counting their trespasses against them (2 Cor 5:19).

nodes.disposition_note: the document names Rom 5:15-20 as a range; G3900 does not occur in 5:19, so the node is the verse alone

findings.text: H6588 (pesha, 58 verses, the single largest strong across all 14 families surveyed so far) shows the same remedy-defined shape: its own meaning block labels sub-senses as recognised by the sinner, as God deals with it, and as God forgives, and the verses bear this out: Ps 32:1 (blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven); Ps 51:1 and 3 (I know my transgressions, my sin is ever before me), the same recognition-language pattern already found in the guilt subgroup's H0816; and Mic 7:18, Isa 43:25 and Isa 44:22, all blotting out or passing over transgression as a divine act.

Isaiah 53:5 (he was pierced for our transgressions) lands in this family at the exact same verse already cited under the guilt subgroup's H5375J and H0817: pesha converges with the bearing and guilt-offering complex at a single shared text.

H6588 runs the same three-register split found in family J (unfaithfulness): its meaning block distinguishes transgression against individuals, nation against nation, and against God, the same structure as H4603 and H4604's against man and against God split. Amos's formula for three transgressions and for four (Amos 1:3 to 2:6) applies pesha at the nation-against-nation register, functioning as an indictment formula against foreign powers, not individual ethics.

H6586 (pasha) fuses transgress and rebel as one verb, and its verses run political revolt (Moab against Israel, Edom against Judah, 2 Kgs 1:1, 3:5, 3:7, 8:22) alongside straightforward religious confession (Lam 3:42, Ps 51:13) without any separation: the same word describes a vassal state revolting from its sovereign and a person confessing sin against God, suggesting the underlying figure is sovereignty and rebellion against a ruler, applied to both political and theological registers alike.
